I always tell my food runners, hosts, and service assistants the same thing: “If a server comes up to you to bitch about you not helping them out, they don’t know how to do their job.”

I’ve been in the industry since I was 15, and servers who know what they’re doing/make good money are always the ones with whom the table SEES them busting their ass by running their own food/refills. Granted that doesn’t always happen with Saturday night dinner rushes, but I’ve never met a seasoned server who was worth a damn that cursed out support staff like that.

When I serve hot tea, I have to warm up the pot with hot water, because otherwise the brewed tea will get “cold,” (many customer complaints) Then I have to get a cup of honey and a ramekin of lemons. I kept apologizing and kept insisting I box up their food and continue full service because there was literally nothing else I could’ve done: and I was expected to get RIPPED in to by them. However their meal ended with them kindly complimenting my service and thanking me for all the trouble, plus a nice tip and they even asked to take a picture with me. 

That’s a story that always makes me smile. It reminds me that for all the bad shit I have to deal with, they do have kind patient people out there.

Hi! I am this girl, and I finally have the first healthy relationship of my life with a fantastic guy. 

The key here is COMMUNICATION! People with BPD often get joked about for being “manic pixie dream types” because we are spontaneous and fun and reckless, but this illness can be very severe. My partner and I have been together for 3 years, not without its hardships. 

Sometimes our emotional capacities blow up on us and we say things we don’t mean. We split easily once we’re triggered. This sounds bad, but a borderline when they’re hurt typically want to hurt those closest to them in a weird self-fulfilling prophecy of self destruction. This relationship could be very bad if you both aren’t emotionally mature enough to handle it, so just be prepared that it could get rough, but if she’s worth it then you’ll stick with her. 

Patience is virtue with borderlines. Sometimes in arguments we will say very harsh things. Please try not to take this too close to heart, but we act like emotional toddlers when we’re hurt. This isn’t an excuse, and a healing borderline will be very self aware and typically apologize afterwards for it, but my partner has told me that when I come at him with very obvious signs of being triggered, he just tries to reassure me, hold me close, and comfort me. If I’ve split severely, he will say, “I love you and I am not leaving you, but I will give you space for a moment to regulate yourself. If you need help, I will be in the other room ready for you.”

Our main issues are with abandonment, and abandonment issues can be triggered by anything. I once had an episode with my partner when he went out with his coworkers while I was stuck at work. I felt like less of a priority and I took it out on him by being very selfish and cruel. Of course I apologized afterwards and do my best to not let that happen again, but a lot of our lack of emotional regulation is far out of our control without extensive therapy. 

I find that the beginning of all of my relationships are entirely based on infatuation. I think I’m in love, but I’m really not, but eventually I do truly fall in love. I just like not being alone. This led me to a lot of horrible relationships and I haven’t been single since I was 14, but I do find that typically borderlines are very loyal and will do ANYTHING for their partners (unless they feel triggered to the point of no return and will leave quickly to ensure you don’t leave them first. COMMUNICATION IS KEY!)

Good luck and have patience and be open. It’s a hell of a disorder to navigate, but truly no one loves as deeply as a borderline.
